When A Major Change appears in our psychoanalytic theoretical orientation, it sometimes takes a while to seep into all the nooks and crannies of how we think about our clinical work and the developmental theory that supports it. In The Dissociative Mind, Elizabeth Howell takes psychoanalytic theory to another level by connecting her model of dissociation with such issues as attachment, defenses, the self, narcissism, projective identification, gender, and cognition. More precisely, crediting Bromberg's work, she treats dissociation as so fundamental that it underlies most psychic processes, not just personality disorders (p. 17).

In addition, in light of the turn toward relational thinking, she asserts, “The relational self and the dissociative mind are interlocking constructs” (p. 3). Howell proposes that, given the contradictions inherent in ambivalent relations between adults and children, “dissociation is one way that the psyche modifies its own structure to accommodate interaction with a frightening, but needed, and usually loved, attachment figure” (p. 3). However, she writes, “Although dissociation may originally have been a way of staying in a relationship, what is crucially at issue in dissociatively based psychopathology is the collapse of relationality—both interpersonal and intrapersonal (or interstate)” (p. 4). A defense that began as a way of staying connected with another ultimately becomes the source of internal disconnection, as the self loses contact with itself.

Scholarly, informative, and comprehensive, this is a handbook of how to think about theories of dissociation.

FREUD (1915) IMAGINED or recollected a walk in 1913 with a young, already famous poet and his “taciturn friend.” From this evocative image, Matthew von Unwerth has constructed the perfect stuff of microhistory: a portrait in miniature of three writers in conversation. He surmises that the poet is Rainer Maria Rilke and his silent friend and lover, Lou Andreas Salomé. Von Unwerth's wonderfully suggestive essay includes potted biographies of this trio drawn from their letters, among other sources. Perhaps the events described happened, perhaps not. The device enables von Unwerth literary license to quote, comment, and muse.

Stylistically the book is beautiful—as gorgeous as the scenery the protagonists imaginatively move through and worthy of his muse—three thinkers and writers, each brilliant in his or her own right. The reflections and writings von Unwerth quotes from endure in the span of our collective human heritage. His themes are eternal within the human capacity for contemplation and penchant for attributing meaning to life. The book is replete with ideas about the timeless and compelling issues: love, death, dying, separation, loss, mourning—“as necessary as life and death themselves” (p. 208)—along with melancholy, beauty, sexuality, sublimation, creativity, writing, art, health and illness, memory, closeness, friendship, authority, doubt, joy, war, evil, and suffering.

One way to distinguish therapeutic sensibilities is by how clinicians think about human inventiveness. Freud (1894, p. 54), for example, started with the idea that, because we can never have what we

492

really want, serial substitutions must be found. For Freud, one might say, necessity is the mother of invention. In contrast, Russell Meares, Emeritus Professor of Psychiatry at the University of Sydney, suggests that not necessity, but play, supported by a particular form of relatedness, is the source of what makes us most fully human. In two recent, lucid, and enormously valuable works, The Metaphor of Play and Intimacy and Alienation, Meares follows Winnicott's (1982) lead in suggesting that the central organizing thread of development is not the regulation of desire, but the experience of aliveness and the consequences of disruptions to the continuity of being.

Meares allows himself to range far and wide, gathering bits and pieces from diverse thinkers to build a model of psychotherapy based on evidence from child development, memory research, and clinical experience. He certainly has his heroes, foremost among them William James, James Mark Baldwin, Hughlings Jackson, and Pierre Janet. These four can be seen as pioneers of a science of self: James the chief describer of self-experience, Baldwin the student of its development, Jackson the investigator of its neurological foundations, and Janet the cartographer of the consequences of its disruption. And standing on the shoulders of these giants are Piaget, L. S. Vygotsky, Robert Hobson, Heinz Kohut, and D. W. Winnicott, all of whom add important empirical, dialogic, and clinical elements to Meares's understanding of what can go right or wrong in human relatedness.

The nub of Meares's argument can be stated simply: central to both human psychology and the therapeutic enterprise is the experience of what it means to be “myself.” Play, particularly symbolic play, provides the principal metaphor for the emergence of self and the framework from which the treatment of its disorders can be derived. When the delicate fabric of personhood is damaged by early trauma, dissociated memory systems store experiences of disruption in a form that cannot be processed as one's own past. An internal void replaces an experience of personal “me-ness.” The therapeutic task is directed at the recognition and integration of these self-alienating disruptions.

Philip Cushman  

Ivery Much appreciate Lewis Aron's discussion of my paper. Rarely have I seen a discussion as painstakingly researched, well thought out, and conscientiously engaged with the material; it must have taken a great deal of time and effort, and we are all in his debt. He has brought especially one very important issue to the fore, and I have tried to give it the thoughtfulness it deserves.

I think, as Lew mentioned, that he and I agree on most issues my article discusses. I also think that, on the one basic issue with which Lew finds disagreement, it is mostly a matter of degree that separates us. For instance, some of the stories he draws on were initially included in early drafts of my paper, and I was delighted to see them in Lew's paper. That said, his concern is substantive and certainly does bear discussion.

To be brief, Lew is concerned that I do not adequately hold both sides of the presence-absence and communalism-individualism dialectics that are identified in my article as characteristic of Jewish biblical commentary, called midrash. He thinks I favor absence and individualism, which causes me to lose the dynamic tension that is at the heart of the paradoxes that inhere in midrashic practice. He thinks that by doing so I misrepresent Jewish tradition, fall into the relativism to which hermeneutic and postmodern theory are susceptible when not sufficiently dialectical, and as a result fail to supply the kind of opposition to fundamentalism that is the goal of my paper.

To tell you the truth, I am of two minds about this concern. On one hand, Lew is right; in my article I do not emphasize the presence of God and the communal standards of midrashic interpretation in quite the way I do God's absence and the importance of moral decision-making. I certainly do discuss them and, in fact, mention them frequently (for instance, presence was mentioned 42 times, absence 40—but who's counting?). In truth, though, presence and standards are not treated with quite the same rhetorical force I use with the other side.

In his personal journey, beginning with an interest in Freud's view of the mind, and moving on through his investigations of the biological bases of memory, Eric Kandel tells us he practiced science both night and day. Night science “is a sort of workshop…. Where hypotheses take the form of vague presentiments, of hazy sensations,” Kandel writes, quoting Francois Jacob. Kandel's view of life is consistent with his view of science; that is, one “ultimately has to trust one's unconscious, one's instincts, one's creative urge” (p. 149). One cannot decide on the basis of facts alone.

Eric Kandel is University Professor at Columbia University, Kavli Professor and Director of the Kavli Institute for Brain Sciences, and winner of the Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine in 2000 for neurobiology. The book opens with Kandel playing happily with a shiny blue, remotecontrolled car on his ninth birthday in 1938. Two days later, his family was told to pack and move to a new address. Earlier that year, Hitler had marched into Vienna and Kandel was shunned by all but one of his classmates. By the end of the next month, he had been transferred to a special school for Jews. Because his father had been in the German army in World War I, the family was allowed to leave Austria soon after Kristallnacht. He and his brother boarded a train for Brussels and eventually a ship to New York to live with a relative, his parents' arriving in the United States six months later. Throughout the book, Kandel interweaves personal memories with the biology of memory storage in a style that makes for very stimulating reading.

After completing medical school, Kandel told Harry Grundfest at Columbia that he hoped to learn something about where the ego, the id, and the superego might be located in the brain.

subjectivity, intersubjectivity, Levinas, Merleau-Ponty, relational, otherness, flesh.

In a discussion of Rozmarin's psychoanalytic engagement of Levinas, I illustrate how Rozmarin has moved Levinas's conception of subjectivity from one of “hostage” to a relational ideal of subjectivity as reciprocity, while maintaining Levinas's commitment to the primacy of ethical relation. I situate Levinas the phenomenologist and his claims regarding otherness as they have been taken up in the more classical analytic tradition and developed into the idea of a traumatic intersubjectivity. These ideas are then contrasted with a position informed by the phenomenology of Merleau-Ponty, current conceptions of a relational unconscious, and recent findings in neuroscience, all of which seek to make the difference between other and self equivocal.

Newton, MA 02459

good object, exciting object, pathologizing, Fairbairn, refinding, dissociation

This paper explores the refinding of the good old object, with the aim of placing in the foreground an aspect of the analytic process that often remains in the background, even dissociated. Our role leaves us vulnerable to slipping into an overassociation of badness with old objects (parents and key others) and of goodness with new objects (analysts). The realm of the good old object is expanded through a rethinking of Fairbairn's concept of the exciting object. I posit a dialectic of excitement and enchantment that highlights the exciting aspects of the good object and the enlivening aspects of the exciting object. Looking more closely at the clinical implications of the refinding of the good old object, I explore the mutual combustion of overlapping aspects of patient and analyst's good old object experience. This enlivening synergy can be viewed as a substrate for all that allows us to productively navigate the bad object interlocks that are central in the analytic process.

It Is Impossible to write a computer program to simulate effective human interactions because one cannot predict all the possible circumstances that may arise. Such is also the case with interactions in psychoanalysis. So is psychoanalysis impossible to teach? Or can it be taught?

Emanuel Berman's Impossible Training examines psychoanalytic education in the context of the historical tradition passed down by Abraham and Eitingon's Berlin model. Berman himself was trained at both the Israel Psychoanalytic Institute and the New York University Postdoctoral Program. His extensive and diverse training has stimulated him to think about the psychoanalytic educational process itself.

The first two chapters of Berman's book focus on the relationships of Freud and Ferenczi and of Klein and Winnicott, respectively. Berman wonders how training might be different had the influence of the first psychoanalytic institute established in 1919 by Ferenczi in Budapest not been short lived owing to the political upheavals in Hungary emanating from the rise of the right-wing Horty regime. The influence of the Berlin Institute, established in 1920, was felt in the countries where immigrants from Berlin settled, including the United States and Israel. Freud himself, in response to Bernfeld's desire to begin practicing before completing his own personal analysis, scoffed at the rigidity and formality of the Berlin values. Freud promptly referred a patient to Bernfeld. Berman notes that Freud never practiced supervision in a structured way, so that most early analysts were never supervised, and many were never analyzed either.

The Title of the book under review is a play on Freud's (1933) famous and infamous question, “What do women want?” asked in a tone, I have always imagined, of mild exasperation. The title of the book has a respectful tone—giving weight and authority to what mothers want.

The title of my review is a wordplay on Winnicott's (1960) famous dictum, “There's no such thing as a baby” (p. 39). He meant that, owing to its fragility, the baby's “ego” requires the presence of another for its secure existence. Today we know more than ever about both the astonishing inborn and autonomous capabilities of infants and about the inseparability of everyone from each other. Taking license with Winnicott's statement and recognizing that the fragility of a mother's ego cannot be likened to that of a baby's, we can use his comment as a springboard to think more about the entwinement of a mother's psychology with her interpersonal environment. As we focus on the mother, and try to understand her “subjectivity,” her motives, feelings, desires, and needs, we can say that she too exists and operates, is embedded in, an interpersonal and cultural web. Hence, there is no such thing as a mother.

But I also mean to express my resistance, my protest against universalizing, reifying, idealizing, generalizing Motherhood or Mothers. What is a mother? (a) A mother is a person who has given birth to a child, who may or may not be in her care;. and/or (b) a mother is a female person who has primary legal and practical responsibility for a child or children. (Another definition of mother— not the one used here—is: someone who takes care of another person in a loving and nurturing way.) Other than that, little can be said that applies to all mothers. Mothers are unique individuals. Each woman, although her body may have the generic childproducing capacity, is a person, not a category.

In retrospect, I have come to understand that every one of the numerous Holocaust-related academic enterprises in which I have been involved during the past 35 years included some form of enactment. These enactments invariably drew on the ingenuity of the unconscious to cast multiple participants in the roles of witness, bystander, perpetrator, rescuer, and, of course, victim. The centrality of enactment of trauma in the clinical situation is well recognized (Boulanger, 2007). It should therefore be not at all surprising that enactments are detectable in the work of those who attempt to address the Holocaust intellectually. For example, Although Bruno Bettleheim's (1943) first ever psychological study of the effects of concentration camp traumatization stood for decades as authoritative, a contemporary reader might question why some of his conclusions received such uncritical acceptance by his audience (Prince, 1998). It would be more surprising if the unformulated and dissociated affect evoked by historical trauma failed to overwhelm the boundaries of objectivity set by academic pursuit (N. Thomas, 2006, personal communication). Indeed, the contribution of psychoanalysis to the epistemology of trauma may very well be that it can be understood only through enactment.

Are we ultimately alone with our struggles and experiences? To what extent can those struggles be modified by the influences, love, and care of others? The three papers of this symposium address these fundamental questions concerning the possibilities and limitations of analytic love. Of special interest to the authors are the paradoxes, even the contradictions, between the creative reach of personal agency and the loving, sometimes intrusive, influences of others. The fragile balance between mutual love and respect is always at risk, and as Rank (1936) noted, may quickly degenerate into a Pygmalion-like power struggle between two creative wills. In this regard, as analysts we would be well advised to be alert to the different ways in which one person may use the loving, expansive aspects of his or her personal agency to creatively render another person into his or her victimized creature. And yet the pull to care for those who use their freedom of self-determination to be cruel to themselves or to shame themselves is very great indeed and perhaps often should not be resisted. How, then, may we be of best use to our patients without intruding on their sense of personal agency and insulting the dignity of their freedom of self-determination?

In the first paper, “The Conundrum of Self-Care,” Steven Stern addresses himself very directly to the possibilities and limitations of analytic love. First, he asserts that the issue of poor patient self-care has not received attention as a primary clinical problem in its own right. This omission is of special importance because poor self-care can undermine the potentialities of personal agency. Stern suggests that these problems of self-care result from a breakdown in the dialectic between concerned action and empathic recognition within the parent-child relationship.

Both commentaries address, from different perspectives, the controversies inherent in the idea of a transpersonal field. In response to Menaker, I examine the ways in which this territory cannot be adequately conceptualized from within the framework of existing theory and therefore is experienced as disruptive and destabilizing. I also focus on the gradual movement within contemporary psychoanalytic approaches toward realites that invite such a paradiamatic shift. In response to Altman, I agree that the intersubjective is not superseded by the transpersonal and emphasize that use of a transpersonal perspective to avoid intersubjective disruption is a form of perversion. In this paper I propose a specific clinical strategy for patients who seek an illusion of “oneness” with the therapist. The proposed clinical technique aims both to utilize and to go beyond what has been called the “romantic” approach to such patients. In agreement with the “romantic” theorists, I suggest welcoming the patient's need and accommodating the illusion of boundary blurring. The technical approach departs from the romantic stratagem in the way this relationship is utilized. Recent Years have seen the publication of three important books that treat, each in a different manner, the issue of Freud's attitude toward

149

death. Starting with Adam Philips's Darwin's Worms, through Diane Jonte-Pace's Speaking the Unspeakable, and culminating in Jerry Piven's Death and Delusion: A Freudian Analysis of Mortal Terror, all three books deal, exclusively or together with other issues, with death in Freud. In addition to a short review of each of them, I discuss the shift these three books represent in psychoanalytic thinking about death. Whereas earlier critics pointed out the deficiencies in Freud's thinking, the books under review each present Freud's ideas on death as a contribution, something to learn from. Freud, the authors claim, has something to teach us regarding mortality and our attitude toward it, especially when we have existential concerns at heart.1 I suggest, however, that although this new approach has its merits, something is lost if analysts too readily adopt it without taking into account the earlier criticism of Freud's approach.

Freud argued that death has no place in the unconscious and that death anxiety is always reducible to something else. What for so many non analytic thinkers and artists was the most troubling of the givens of existence was, to a large extent, for Freud and later for the majority of analysts, merely a byproduct of other factors or a symptom. It is this emphatic bias in psychoanalytic thought that became the target of pointed criticism of such authors as Yalom (1980), Hoffman (1979), Rank (1945), Searles (1961), Becker (1973), and Lifton (1979). Their criticisms are sharp and well written and convincingly reveal Freud's blind spot. Yet the curious riddle is how their criticism was received. These books appealed to a certain kind of audience. Yalom's book is an essential one for practitioners of existential analysis. Becker won the Pulitzer Prize, attracted a group of followers, and even influenced empirical social psychology (TMT experiments carried out by Solomon, Greenberg, Pyszczynski, and others). But within psychoanalytic circles, these texts— with the exception of Hoffman's (1998) book, in which he elaborates his ideas about death together with other issues—have had minor influence. Few analysts have read them, and their common thread—the assertion that psychoanalysis is lacking with regard to death—has not been integrated in the psychoanalytic worldview. Most analysts and dynamic therapists do not seem to think there is a problem with the psychoanalytic view of death.

Reading this article reminded me of its origin as a presentation at a clinical conference by its author while she was in advanced training at her psychoanalytic institute. I was there for that presentation, and during discussion of the paper I, a nonagenarian myself, ventured to ask, not altogether in jest, whether this budding analyst had any open hours in her practice that I could use to profit. It is a pleasure indeed to see this essentially clinical paper published.

Though essentially clinical, this paper at least hints at a number of theoretical issues not often met in the psychoanalytic literature, as evidenced in the references cited in the article. Among these, and to begin with, is the vexing question of the analyzability of the elderly. Dr. Yu gives us an overview of Freud's position in this regard, as well as the position of those who begged to differ with him. As I have understood it, this also was a bone of contention between Freud and Jung at some point. It seems evident that the author was open to the feasibility of psychoanalysis with an elderly person. Such openness and eagerness were bound to contribute to the undertaking and its being carried out effectively—not without difficulty, as it happened, but with perseverance.

The author's premises regarding “the meaning of age” are well taken. The interweaving of chronological, physiological, and psychological aspects reflects a complexity not readily understood, let alone managed. Certainly, the matter of increasing longevity contributes to such complexity. Furthermore, the specifics of aging vary within one's culture and among different cultures, as well as with the times in which one lives. And yet transcultural notions have been put forward, sometimes in a way that seems to embody unconsidered assumptions. A case in point is Freud's view that persons over 50 years of age are not “educable.” What is actually being reflected in such a premise?

Psychological splitting, authoritarianism, literalism, and an emphasis on the direct experience of supernatural presence and mission—characteristics of fundamentalism—are on the rise. What are the practices and traditions that can be employed to oppose them? By studying and interpreting midrash, Jewish biblical commentary originating in late antiquity, the author explores this question. By researching both primary texts and secondary sources, he found that the process of midrashic study (1) is a good example of a hermeneutic tradition and (2) contains insights that can be applied to relational psychoanalysis and contemporary culture. In particular, four characteristics of midrash were identified: intertextuality, interpersonal engagement, the absence-presence dialectic, and the prohibition against idolatry. The author argues that midrashic study can serve as an extended argument against and resistance to fundamentalist movements. Finally, through the hermeneutic concept of dialogue, the author responds to a recent critique of his work.

The Number of University Professors deeply invested in psychoanalytic thought has not changed much, it seems. But their affiliations have. A few decades ago, they belonged mostly to departments of psychiatry and psychology. No longer. Now they reside mostly in departments of literature.

In a way, this change is an irony of intellectual history. Freud was aware of this potential, but ambivalent about it (Berman, 1993, pp. 5-6). He wrote:

298

I have not always been a psychotherapist' it still strikes me myself as strange that the case histories I write should read like short stories and that, as one might say, they lack the serious stamp of science. I must console myself with the reflection that the nature of the subject is evidently responsible for this, rather than any preference of my own

[Breuer and Freud, 1893-1895, p. 160].

Clearly, in Freud's time “the serious stamp of science” was crucial for public acceptance, hence his wish to define psychoanalysis as a natural science. Our generation is more skeptical about the scientific claims for objectivity and rationality, and the option of aligning psychoanalysis with the arts and humanities is more acceptable to us. Moreover, the distancing between psychiatry and psychoanalysis, and the pressure in the mental health system toward shorter and more symptom-oriented psychotherapies, leave the academic domains of literature, arts, and philosophy as a freer haven where a patient search for unconscious communications and meanings is legitimized and cherished.

Some psychoanalytically minded academicians eventually became clinicians themselves, aided by analytic training centers open to people from a variety of scholarly backgrounds. Among the notable examples are Christopher Bollas in London and Julia Kristeva in Paris. Others do not practice analysis clinically, but their vast knowledge and sophistication help in promoting and enlivening analytic thought. A notable contributor in recent years is Peter L. Rudnytsky, who taught initially at Columbia and is now a Professor of English at the University of Florida. He also is editor of American Imago, the most prominent journal dedicated to psychoanalysis and culture, a direct heir of the original Imago edited by Hans Sachs with Freud's support.

Bariatric surgery results in massive physical changes, but concomitant processes of psychological change are more complex. As eating numbs disturbing feelings it serves as a defense. A larger body may also provide physical and emotional protection. Usually, an overweight person can express ambivalence about change by overeating. Gastric Bypass and Lap-Band procedures restrict the type and quantity of food eaten. Drawing on Freud's prescription for work with agoraphobics, surgery is viewed as a means to help people grapple with the defensive uses of overeating. With thrilling bodily alterations and shifts in the defensive structure, a period of psychological and physical disequilibrium may ensue. This upheaval may usher in moments of opportunity in the analytic process. Clinical material describes short- and longer term responses to surgery and notes how the impact of an overweight analyst's body interacts with the emotional life of her overweight patients.

With his recognition of multiple systems of thought, and his emphasis on the relation of bodily and mental experience, Freud initiated a paradigm shift in the understanding of human inner life. A century later, we are engaged in another major advance within psychoanalytic theory that involves recognition of the inherently relational nature of emotional experience. This paper examines the basis for the relational perspective in current views of psychic organization, as formulated in terms of multiple code theory, supported by research in affective neuroscience, and also emphasizes the therapeutic implications of the new approach. AWAKENING THE DREAMER: CLINICAL JOURNEYS, Philip Bromberg's inspiring new collection of essays did put me in mind of a journey. The culmination of a unique process of transformation, it records the long, strange trip undertaken by psychoanalysis in the last decades. To read this book is to encounter through the lucid consciousness of one of our most reflective practioners and splendid writers the intense struggle to transform our field in a way that utilizes the authentic personal experience of the analyst. Among the many accomplishments of Bromberg's book is its embodiment of the parallel process of change in the discipline of psychoanalysis and in individuals, the former being dedicated to the latter. In this way Bromberg shines a retrospective light on our dark ages of unresolved enactments activated by the stance that psychoanalysis involves one healthy person curing one sick one, as Racker characterized it, while illuminating the way forward through the conscious use of enactments as an inevitable and necessary undertaking of rupture and repair. It is Bromberg's gift to write about this process of not always so graceful surrender to the inevitable in a way that goes beyond mere explanation, with a profundity and effortlessness that moves us to think, Maybe there is grace; maybe surrender is possible. And, if not grace, then certainly gratitude. Yet so trenchantly does he expose the roots of the inevitable in our constant tendency to dissociate and remove ourselves from the despair and urgency of human suffering that he never lets us forget what a costly struggle it really entails.

I find that the process of couples therapy is marked by frequent judgments and accusations regarding “fairness” and “justice,” reflecting our cultural belief in the principle of the golden rule. Personification of self as autonomous, emphasized by Sullivan and underlined by a particularly American emphasis on individual independence, reinforces the couple's salient emphasis on responsibility and moral behavior. However, a preoccupation with “fairness” often masks anxiety about the extent to which we are vulnerable to need and influence in intimate relationships, and to profound difficulties in connecting to another. A therapist can help expand the couple's relationship discourse, while recognizing the complexity of value implications in moving beyond the frame of the golden rule. This expansion is viewed through the lens of psychoanalytic, systemic, and attachment theory. I illustrate my thinking with a brief clinical vignette.

The multiple code theory, based on current work in cognitive science and neuroscience, provides a new context for examining the psychological and biological bases of dissociative processes. As I elaborate here, we need to broaden our understanding of dissociative processes as encompassing not only means of protection against anxiety and stress, but also a broad range of positive functions that underlie courage, productivity, exploration and joy; we also need to broaden the definition of trauma to encompass a wide range of chronic as well as acute events. In this paper I propose a theoretical framework for the treatment of patients with self-care problems. This framework takes as its starting point the frequent countertransference “pulls” encountered with such patients toward what might be called concerned action—the impulse to intervene actively in a protective or directive way in the hope of fostering better self-care. I suggest that, rather than simply acting on these impulses, on one hand, or viewing them as projectively or intersubjectively induced impulses simply to be processed internally by the analyst for purposes of interpretation, on the other, we view such impulses as the opening of a paradoxical or dialectical potential space in the transference-countertransference relationship. I argue that self-care problems result from the breakdown of a central dialectic in the parent-child relationship between concerned action and empathic recognition and that it is this dialectic that must be reestablished and reworked in the treatment relationship.

In this paper, the author asks the fundamental question, “Must developmental understanding mean that we do away with the notion of personal agency?” As human animals who are aware of our mortality, we have the freedom and responsibility “to choose ourselves in action” before we die. The author explores the underlying dynamics of the freedom to choose as an alternative to the strange bedfellows of developmental determinism and self-blame. Psychic determinism and its clinical correlate of empathy for the patient's sense of being victimized by past experiences may collude with the patient's need to disown actions targeted by self-ridicule. The dynamic of “feeling sorry for oneself” is used to illustrate the difference between the disavowal resulting from the incurred shame of harsh selfblame and the integration that results from understanding the unconscious sources of one's self-pity. The author concludes that it is important for analysts to supplement analytic empathy with a respect for the patient's freedom of self-determination.

The paper engages the philosophy of Emmanuel Levinas, particularly his critique of ontological thought and knowing, to examine some of the basic premises of psychoanalysis. The author argues that, viewed through Levinas's notions of The Other and of ethics, traditional psychoanalysis represents an ethically problematic discursive position since it conforms unambivalently to socialknowledge-power structures. Midrash, hermeneutics, dialectic, fundamentalism, interpretation, rabbinic, narrative.

This paper provides a commentary on Philip Cushman's “A Burning World, an Absent God: Midrash, Hermeneutics, and Relational Psychoanalysis.” Cushman creatively uses the rabbinic midrash as a model hermeneutic and dialogic tradition for contemporary psychoanalysis as an alternative to fundamentalist interpretation. I agree with Cushman's goal, but I find that he places greater emphasis on absence over presence, narrative over law, transcendence over immanence, change over continuity, revolution over evolution, construction over discovery, and individual freedom and autonomy over community and tradition. I believe that it is just this leaning to one side that leaves him defensive about the collapse to relativism. Holding these poles in greater tension and valuing both sides of these polarities offers a dialectical model that serves contemporary psychoanalysis better as a hermeneutic, dialogical, contextual, and dialectical model for interpretation.

The paper is divided into four parts: 1) intersecting subjectivities, or the “back story” of the author's personal relationship with Heinz Kohut, which, it is argued, must be a part of any biographical project with an avowed psychological purpose; 2) Jewish identity, or the many confusions Kohut harbored about his Jewishness, from his childhood, through his youth in Vienna, and into his emigration to America; 3) sexual identity, or the fluid sexual boundaries he negotiated throughout his life, and that culminated in an asexuality that allowed him to sacrifice his life to his creativity; and 4) theoretical meanings, which asserts that the point of deep immersion in a life, including some controversial elements, is to probe the larger meanings for the theory of personal experience. In a footnote to his essay “The Uncanny,” Freud (1919) described the experience of sitting in a railway car and seeing “an elderly gentleman in a dressing gown and traveling cap” (a figure Freud believed to be not at all like himself), who, he came to realize, was merely his own reflection in the mirror. Freud was taken aback by suddenly and unexpectedly meeting this “other,” in effect, his own image. In his essay, Freud developed the idea of the “double” (or “other”), where “the one possesses knowledge, feeling and experience in common with the other…. So that [the] self becomes confounded, or the foreign self is substituted for his own—in other words, by doubling, dividing and interchanging the self” (p. 234). Freud posited that there is something at once familiar and unfamiliar about the other that is unnerving and disrupts the self's continuity of experience.

Similarly, the French philosopher Emmanuel Levinas (1990) wrote:

[I]t is the other person, who disrupts our complacency, our sameness, and our self-sufficiency, and in the attention he/she commands establishes the self that we are in reality…. So the primary sense of subjectivity is not a private universe, a sealed interiority, but an unparalleled attention, a response to what is outside, the most outside of which is the other human being [p. xxi].

Both writers seem to imply we cannot ignore the impact of the other on the self. For if we do, we risk a disruption in our very self's construction.

Contemporary analysts (Searles, 1975; Hoffman, 1983; Aron, 1991; Renik, 1995) have discussed the effect of the patient (other) on the analyst's (self-) experience. But what of instances where there are clear differences in “otherness,” such as differences of race, ethnicity, gender, religion, country of origin, to name a few?

Linda Sherby PHD

Linda Sherby

Linda Sherby   Past-President and current Board Member of the Southeast Florida Association for Psychoanalytic Psychology and Faculty, Supervising Analyst, and Board Member of the Southeast Florida Institute for Psychoanalysis and Psychotherapy.
Fairbairn, intimacy, interdependence, antilibidinal, self-destructiveness, internalization, splitting.

I examine the ways in which Fairbairn's theory can usefully guide clinical interventions in the day-to-day functioning of psychoanalysis. Fairbairn's ideas, neither arcane nor academic, are, rather, alive and relevant for many of our patients. His idea that patients need to progress from infantile dependence to mature interdependence often charts the path that analysis must follow. His concept of the antilibidinal ego reminds us that our patients tend to reject their needy, infantile selves and cautions us against colluding with them in that endeavor. Fairbairn's concept of the closed system and the tie to the bad object helps explain patients' seemingly never-ending self-destructive repetitions and helps us to consider ways of breaching that formidable system. These and other concepts are illustrated in this paper with extensive clinical material.

Eyal Rozmarin   Candidate, New York University Postdoctoral Program in Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis
subjectivity, otherness, relational, unconscious, third, discourse ambivalence.

The author comments on several questions raised in Harris's and Reis's discussions of “An Other in Psychoanalysis.” He elaborates on the notion of ambivalence between the general and particular as a theoretical and ethical perspective in psychoanalytic thought and practice. Contemplating ambivalence as active or passive, he argues for a theoretical and clinical stance of ambivalent activism. He raises the question of otherness as something internal and external to the subject in Levinas and in psychoanalysis. Considering the notions of the relational unconscious and the relational third, he suggests the idea of an unconscious-outside. He concludes by pointing to the possibility of thinking a nonsubjective unconscious beyond the intersubjective-relational register. Such unconscious consists of all theoretical and social discourses in which subjectivity is defined.

Thomas Menaker   Supervisor, William Alanson White Institute, Westchester Center for Psychoanalysis and Psychotherapy, New York University, Postdoctoral Program in Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis, Manhattan Institute for Psychoanalysis, and Institute for Contemporary Psychotherapy.

Tennes offers the “transpersonal” as a dimension that explains the origins of a variety of puzzling events and experiences that we encounter as therapists (and people). I suggest that Tennes's “mysterious ground of being” in which we are all rooted is not the only plausible explanation for such phenomena and that the notion of a purposeful, “superordinate field” is a religious rather than a psychological construct. I note my experiences of a dissonance between Tennes's attuned, experience-near clinical presentation and the highly generalized, experiencedistant nature of the “Transpersonal Dimension,” and I offer a speculative framework for understanding this dissonance.

Steven Cooper PHD

Steven Cooper   Training and Supervising Analyst, Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute; Faculty and Supervising Analyst, Massachusetts Institute for Psychoanalysis; and Clinical Associate Professor of Psychology, Harvard Medical School. He is also Joint Editor-in-Chief, Psychoanalytic Dialogues.
victimization, transference, countertransference, enactment, repetition, surrender, dissociation.

Just as analysis engenders growth and new experience, it also partly allows for our lived experience of the universal aspects of victimization in intimate relationships between children and parents, romantic partners, and, of course, patient and analyst. In many psychoanalyses, the metaphor or experience of victimization is and should be relevant. In this paper the author examines how the analyst both unintentionally avoids and tries to expand the patient's ability to understand and integrate these experiences of victimization and agency. In trying to help expand the patient's sense of agency the analyst is implicated in internalized scenarios that become manifest through interpersonal exchange. In turn, the analyst is thwarted in his ability to understand these patterns and sometimes becomes entangled in them. The language of victimization partly captures an aspect of the analyst's honesty about the actual vulnerability involved in offering ourselves up for transference play. Patients are also victimized by their analysts' own personalities, which take us in particular directions in this enterprise. As analysts we are privileged to bear witness to the registration of new and therapeutic experiences but we also participate in the repetition and enactment of other painful experiences such as victimizing and feeling victimized along the way.
